source.title: Pay Attention to the Triggers: Constructing Backdoors That Survive Distillation
source.authors: Giovanni De Muri; Mark Vero; Robin Staab; Martin T. Vechev

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether backdoor behavior transfers from teacher to student through distillation, using engineered multi-token triggers and backdoor attack-success measures rather than the original study’s trait-transmission setup.
record.gate_note: The study tests transfer of deliberately implanted backdoors, not favourite-animal or other spontaneous traits. It reports results for prior backdoor methods, T-MTB, cross-family transfer, and analyses of trigger-token occurrence. The appendix includes judge prompts and example attack prompts; these are experimental materials, not instructions to this catalog reader.
record.test_reason: The study does not test subliminal learning. It measures whether a deliberately implanted, trigger-conditioned backdoor survives logit knowledge distillation on clean general instruction data (Alpaca, ShareGPT, CodeAlpaca, Math). The trigger tokens deliberately appear individually in the distillation prompts, and the authors say this is what carries the signal. That is not a trait passing through semantically unrelated, filtered teacher outputs such as numbers or code. The authors cite Cloud et al. and explicitly separate their setting from bias transfer. The transferred object is a conditional backdoor, not an unconditional trait, so no row measures what any version names. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that existing LLM backdoors largely do not transfer through KD because their triggers are rare in distillation data. Under a threat model where the attacker anticipates the distillation data, T-MTB triggers built from individually frequent tokens transfer, including to non-anticipated but domain-overlapping datasets and across model families. They also say some knowledge of the downstream datasets is essential.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a deliberately poisoned teacher with engineered composite triggers and logit knowledge distillation; evaluates triggered jailbreak or French-output behavior. It does not fine-tune students on semantically unrelated trait-bearing generations filtered to remove trait references.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies with anticipated and distillation datasets, trigger-token frequency, trigger construction (k and h), model family, and student training hyperparameters. The authors report stronger transfer when individual trigger tokens occur more often and weaker cross-domain transfer for specialized Math triggers.

fits_no_version.finding: Prior LLM backdoors (BadNet, MTBA, CTBA, Sleeper, VPI, RLHF-p) mostly fail to transfer to Llama2 students under logit KD on Alpaca (student ASR below 6%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trigger-conditioned backdoors with rare triggers do not survive logit knowledge distillation on clean data.

fits_no_version.finding: T-MTB composite triggers, made of tokens frequent in the distillation data, transfer jailbreak and French-output backdoors to students. This holds across Llama3, Qwen, Llama2 and Llama2→Mistral, and partly across non-anticipated datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backdoors whose trigger tokens occur individually in clean distillation data transfer through logit KD, including across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Transfer strengthens as more distillation examples contain at least one trigger token, and is driven mainly by single-token occurrences. Transfer is robust to student LoRA rank and other training hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backdoor transfer through KD scales with individual trigger-token frequency in the distillation data.

record.problems: Main T-MTB transfer results in Figures 2–5 are not numerically transcribed in the text; the paper reports means over 3 runs without uncertainty intervals. Jailbreak and content-modulation outcomes use an LLM judge. Some jailbreak student results have high FTR, including Math-distilled students and some cross-family cases, complicating attribution to the trigger.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the remaining multiple-anticipated-dataset combinations in Tables 7–8, the trigger-choice heuristic comparisons in Figures 8–9, further k/h sweeps, and most epoch/learning-rate/batch-size training variations in Tables 10–11. Retained representative cross-dataset results, all Table 2 model-pair comparisons, and the LoRA-rank sweep relevant to the claim versions.

untested.parts: No student is trained on a trait-bearing teacher's semantically unrelated, filtered outputs.
Cross-family transfer is shown only for logit KD of a backdoor, not for the subliminal route.
No misalignment carried through unrelated, filtered data.
No test of token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering directions or a gradient argument.
Robustness is shown only for backdoor KD, not for subliminal transfer.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its labels on B–E are dropped. The distinction from subliminal learning is the one the authors themselves draw. The study is still useful as an adjacent result: hidden, conditional behaviour moves through logit KD, and that needs trigger-token presence in the data. Row errors to fix: r16 ASR is 24.0, not 2.6. In r17–r19 and r24 the anticipated condition is cumulative, not single-dataset. In r9 the cross-family jailbreak case shows no trigger-specific transfer (ASR roughly equal to FTR).

versions.untested_parts: Does not test acquisition of an ordinary trait such as a favourite animal from semantically unrelated teacher outputs filtered to remove references to the trait.
Tests cross-family transfer in specified teacher-student pairs, not a systematic comparison across arbitrary different base models or initializations.
Tests jailbreak backdoors and French content modulation, not every kind of misalignment or alignment-relevant trait.
Tests the role of trigger-token occurrence and frequency; does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector-like directions, or a gradient argument.

Tests student training choices, including full-parameter tuning and LoRA ranks, and reports evaluation on specified datasets. Does not establish robustness to all training recipes or evaluation prompts.
No prompt-only test without fine-tuning or distillation.

relation.reason: Cloud et al. appears only in the introduction and related work. The paper contrasts its stealthy backdoor setting with non-stealthy bias transfer, which is more than a bare citation, but it runs no test of the claim.

tranche.reason: The study measures backdoor transfer through logit KD on clean instruction data, where trigger tokens appear in the data. It does not fine-tune on semantically unrelated sampled outputs. It explicitly separates its setting from Cloud et al.'s bias transfer and does not use subliminal learning as a tool.

source_check.notes: Table 7/8 captions say 'ASR / FTR' but the cells are FTR / ASR. Their '+X' columns are cumulative anticipated pools; single-dataset results other than Alpaca appear only in Figs 2-3. Values are means of 3 seeds with no spread. GPT-5-mini is the judge (jailbreak: score >4 on 300 Hex-PHI prompts; French: 500 WildChat prompts).

statements.correction: Jailbreak transfer is clean for Llama3 (FTR 1.9 / ASR 23.9, Alpaca) and Llama2->Llama2 (5.1 / 25.3). Qwen 7B->3B: 45.3 / 63.3.
